title: Notifications that earn their interruption
excerpt: Interrupt only when someone must act or would be angry to miss it. Everything else waits in a log. A product that pings for its own activity gets muted.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The quiet fits a piece about interrupting only when the message has earned it.
caption: Most events can wait in a log. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a product interrupt someone?
faqs.answer: Interrupt when they must do something only they can do, or when they would be angry to hear the news late. A failed payment, a waiting approval, and a suspicious sign-in qualify. Edits, feature announcements, and activity summaries can wait in a log they open on purpose.

faqs.question: What should the notification say?
faqs.answer: One sentence that names what happened and one action they can take, using the same names as the product. Include a date when timing changes the meaning. Opening the notification should land on that decision, not on a generic home screen.

faqs.question: How do you keep people from muting everything?
faqs.answer: Give separate controls for each type of event, with an example sentence, so billing warnings can stay on while document edits go quiet. Keep security and billing honest if an admin cannot turn them off. A single switch labeled Notifications trains people to silence the real warnings along with the noise.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Notification design is a rule about interruption: ping only when the person must do something, or would be angry to have missed it. Everything else can wait in a log they open on purpose. A product that pings for its own activity gets muted, and the mute takes the real warnings with it.

Write the rule down before you add another event. If you cannot say which of the two tests a message passes, it does not get a sound, a badge, or a push. It gets a line in the log.

## Two reasons to interrupt, and a log for the rest

The first reason is a task only they can finish. A payment that failed and will lock the account. An invite that is waiting on their approval. A mention that asks them a question. A security event, such as a new sign-in from a place they do not recognize. These are interrupts. Delay has a cost they would notice.

The second reason is news they would be angry to hear late. The export they requested is ready, and it contains customer data they are waiting on. A deploy they started has failed. A teammate has removed their access. The test is anger, not delight. "You might find this interesting" fails the test.

Everything else waits. Someone edited a doc they are not in. The product shipped a feature. A weekly summary of activity they can see by opening the home screen. A badge that counts those events trains people to clear badges without reading. Then the failed payment sits in the same pile.

Keep one log, in the product, in reverse time order, with the unread state separate from the interrupt. The log is where low-stakes events live. It is also where interrupts remain after they have been seen, so a person can find Tuesday's approval without scrolling a chat with the product.

Nielsen Norman Group, in [research on how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), found that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that the first 10 seconds decide whether the page earns more of their time. An interruption spends that same scarce attention. It pulls them out of the page they chose. If the message does not survive a 10-second reading, it should not have pulled them at all. Jakob Nielsen's write-up is about page visits, and the lesson for notifications is narrower: you are borrowing time they had already given to something else.

## Write the sentence they can act on

Each interrupt is one sentence plus one action. What happened. What they should do. The object, named the way it is named in the product.

"The card for Northwind failed. Update billing before Friday if you want the workspace to stay editable." That is an interrupt. "Something went wrong with your account" is an alarm with no door.

"Alex asked you to approve the new member, Priya." The action is Approve or Review. "You have a new notification" is the product talking about itself.

Put the action on the notification. Opening it should land on the decision, not on a home screen that hopes they remember why they came. If the action can be done safely inline, do it there, and write the result back into the log. If it cannot, deep-link to the exact record.

Time belongs in the sentence when time changes the meaning. "Before Friday" is content. "Just now" on a message they will see tomorrow is noise. Use a date.

The W3C describes [WCAG 2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) as a shared standard so more people can use web content. One piece of that standard, status messages, asks that a status be available to assistive technology without forcing keyboard focus onto it. That is the technical version of the same restraint. A confirmation that a file saved can be announced and logged. It does not need to steal the place they were typing. Reserve focus changes for the events that truly require a decision.

## Choose the channel after the rule, not before

Channels are volume knobs. They are not a reason to invent events.

In the product, a banner or a badge is enough for something they will see because they are already there. Use a banner for the task that blocks the current work. Use the log for the rest. A modal is for the rare case where continuing would do harm, such as leaving with an unsaved billing change that would lock the team. A modal for "we updated the app" spends a modal you may need later.

Email is for events they might need while they are away, and for a record they may search for. The failed payment, the export, the access change. Email is a poor channel for high-frequency activity. If you would not want five of them in an hour, batch them or keep them in the log.

Push, on a phone, is the loudest interrupt you have. It has to pass both tests and still be wanted on a Saturday. Security and "the thing you were waiting for is ready" can earn it. Feature announcements do not. Ask for push permission after a person has done something that makes the push obvious, such as starting an export they will want when they leave their desk. A permission prompt on the first launch, before they care, teaches them to refuse, and you will not get a second easy chance.

Digest is a channel. A morning note that lists what waited overnight can replace a dozen pings, if the digest itself is short and the items link to the decision. A digest that repeats the marketing site is an interrupt in a slower costume.

## What gets muted, and how to recover

People mute products that cry wolf. The mute is rational. Your job is to notice it in the design, before the operating system does it for them.

Give a per-type control. They should be able to turn off "edits to documents" without turning off "billing failures." A single switch labeled Notifications is how the failed payment goes silent. Label the types in their language, and show an example sentence so they know what they are keeping.

Do not hide the security and billing types in a submenu that looks optional. You can still let an admin force those on for the workspace. Say that you have done so. A control that pretends to turn off a payment warning, and does not, is a lie. A control that explains "Billing alerts stay on for admins" is a rule.

When someone has muted a type, respect it. The log still records the event. The next interrupt they have allowed should be obviously different, so the channel still means something.

Re-asking for permission every session is another form of noise. If they refused push, wait until a real event would have used it, and offer it once, in a sentence that names the event. "Exports can ping you when the file is ready" is a reason. "Enable notifications to stay in the loop" is the product asking for attention in general.

## A matrix you can keep on one page

Make a table for the events you actually send. Four columns are enough: event, why it qualifies, channel, what the sentence says.

- Failed payment: they must act, and they would be angry to miss it. Email and an in-product banner. The date access changes.
- Export ready: they asked for it. In-product, plus email if they have left. A link to the file, and when the link expires.
- New sign-in: they would be angry to miss it. Email. What to do if it was not them.
- Comment that asks a question: they may need to act. In-product, email if they are not here. The comment, truncated, and a link to the spot.
- Teammate edited a file: neither test. Log only.
- Product news: neither test. A changelog they can open. Not a badge.

If a row has a channel and a blank "why," delete the channel. If you cannot write the sentence without the words "just checking in," the event is not ready.

Review the matrix when you add a feature. New features arrive with a desire to be announced. The matrix is the place that desire has to pass a test. Add the log line first. Add the interrupt only if one of the two reasons is true.

## Quiet hours and the person who lives in the tool

A team that lives in the product all day will feel every badge. Default to quiet. Let them opt into more, type by type, once they know what the types are.

Quiet hours are a mercy for push and email. Let a person set a window, and hold non-security messages until it opens. Security still goes. Say that in the setting, so the window is not a false promise the night a sign-in looks wrong.

Do not use motion to make a low-stakes event feel important. A bouncing icon is an interrupt made out of animation. If the event failed the test, it does not get the bounce either.

Read a day of your own notifications from the product, out loud. If you would mute yourself, the matrix is wrong. Fix the rows before you add a new channel.

The practical next step is the file people ask for when they do not trust the tool to be the only copy. [A settings export a team can trust](/blog/a-settings-export-a-team-can-trust) explains how to say what the file contains, how fresh it is, and when it will arrive. An export that finishes with no sentence is the kind of event your matrix should have refused to leave in silence, and also refused to celebrate.

If you want help deciding which events deserve a sound, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of messages you send today. The useful work is crossing most of them off.
